note: An inventory of bounded claims and the CI jobs that back them. `gates` are jobs the single required check ci-required needs, so they run on every pull request; `scheduled_gates` run only on the schedule or manual dispatch. Evidence of record is a CI run of those jobs on the pinned toolchain (each uploads its logs as an artifact retained 90 days); local runs are informative only. `evidence_run` and `scheduled_evidence_run` name the latest green run of the gates when the entry was last updated: a push run on main, and for the scheduled gates a manual dispatch run that may be on a branch whose tree equals main's (formal/README.md names the commit). Reference validation is textual, not semantic proof.

claims.claim: The Lean model gives seal binding and closed DAG/checkpoint history under its honest-signer assumption; every hash-dependent conclusion is in explicit-witness form (equal bodies, or a SHA-256 collision on the two specific framed preimages), the standard reduction to SHA-256 collision resistance.
assumptions: SHA-256 collision resistance (never assumed as injectivity; explicit collision witnesses)
Ed25519 unforgeability, stated as a hypothesis about which messages were signed
honest signer
model inputs are post-NFC (Unicode NFC is trusted)
Lean 4.30.0 kernel

claims.claim: Rust matches the executable Lean preimage oracle on a fixed corpus and tag inventory; this is sampled conformance, not a mechanized refinement proof.
assumptions: corpus covers the relevant drift
Lean model expresses the intended format

claims.claim: The production seal core (canonical serializer, LP framing, sha256 digest string, record/checkpoint preimages and hashes, signature message) is extracted from core/src by Charon/Aeneas and proved to compute the Lean model's definitions; the model's explicit-witness seal theorems are applied to it (equal hashes give the same body or a SHA-256 collision on the two specific production preimages). Partial correctness only (results when the extracted function returns Ok; a panic or error yields no hash); arithmetic overflow panics in every shipped profile (overflow-checks in release and server, default in dev), matching the model's failure on overflow. serialize()'s final from_utf8 and the PreimageFault-to-RecordError mapping are unextracted glue pinned by call-path checks; base64 (core/src/b64.rs) is excluded as off the hashed/signed path and covered by plan 011's Kani proofs; the verifier's decision logic is refined only in its claim kernel (see verdict-kernel-refinement).
assumptions: Charon/Aeneas/Lean 4.31 toolchain, mathlib and the Aeneas std models (pinned in manifest.json)
rustc (exact pinned nightly for extraction; 1.92.0 for builds)
NFC and SHA-256 as arbitrary functions (unicode-normalization incl. its ASCII fast path; sha2)
String/str UTF-8 model
overflow-checks enabled in the shipped profiles
Ed25519 as the model's Signed hypothesis

claims.claim: The verifier's claim kernel verify::verdict::decide_claims (every function it calls, including the seal-key and anchor searches, the revocation-mode, capstone and plan 009 historical conditions) is extracted from core/src by Charon/Aeneas and proved to return, for every claim and the requested one, exactly the Lean verdict model's decideClaim on any evidence state its checked facts correspond to (Refinement.Corresponds). The model's support-erasure and claim-order theorems (deleting supporting attachments never adds a satisfied claim and never changes a refutation, with fixed signed records, pins, policy and authenticated adverse evidence), Supports inversion, capstone prerequisites, committed-contradiction refutation and the historical results hold for the production results. Total correctness, standard axioms only (enforced per declaration of the verdict modules and the extracted kernel by ProductionAudit.lean). Not proved: that verify.rs computes facts satisfying the correspondence (signature, pin, join, Merkle-path and snapshot passes, counter-to-fact joins); that boundary is pinned by call-path checks and tested by the verdict oracle differential and the adversarial suite.
assumptions: Charon/Aeneas/Lean toolchain and Aeneas std models
rustc
String::is_empty model
verify.rs computes facts satisfying Refinement.Corresponds

proofs.symbol: deletion strengthens a required trust claim

claims.claim: The production RCP parser (CanonValue::parse via parse_typed/parse_document and every function it calls) is extracted from core/src by Charon/Aeneas and proved to return for every byte string of any length (Refinement.Parse.parse_document_total): no panic, arithmetic overflow, out-of-bounds index or divergence. Hypothesis NfcFits (the trusted NFC primitive returns representable Rust strings), never an axiom. The theorem holds in Aeneas' std model: Rust Vec capacity overflow (a panic above isize::MAX bytes, reachable on wasm32 by one string of more than about 2^29 UTF-16 units), allocation failure and stack depth are not modelled; the verifier rejects bundles over MAX_BUNDLE_BYTES (256 MiB) before parsing, while the options JSON and the standalone canonicalize export are uncapped and rely on their callers. Not proved: which documents it accepts or what they parse to (tests, fuzzing, the parser differential and plan 011's Kani families cover that), the error rendering into_public, and NFC's own panic-freedom. Supersedes the unverified Kani harness parse_never_panics as panic-freedom evidence. The parser mutants m60-m64 are run against the regenerated proof (the CI job formal-production) on every pull request.
assumptions: Charon/Aeneas/Lean 4.31 toolchain and the Aeneas std models (unbounded Vec capacity, infallible allocation, unbounded stack)
input size bounded by the caller (MAX_BUNDLE_BYTES in the verify path)
NFC as an arbitrary function whose outputs fit in usize::MAX bytes (NfcFits hypothesis)
SHA-256 as an arbitrary function

claims.claim: Kani proves, only within each harness's stated bounds, properties of the real Rust: base64url alphabet bijection; base64url tail and 4-symbol chunk canonicality over the full per-chunk domains (whole-string uniqueness is argued in prose from the chunking, not proved); sha256:<hex> digest-string injectivity and canonicality per byte; exact LP framing; member-key order equal to UTF-16 code-unit order for keys of one or two scalars (5 of 5 harnesses) and transitive for single-scalar keys; the strict UTF-16 decoder equal to std's on every 1- and 2-unit sequence; the typed integer round trip for every n in [-99,999, 99,999]; canonical spelling of every accepted numeric literal of 1 to 4 bytes (61 of 61 shards); write_string then the real parser (real NFC) returns exactly Str(s) for every string of at most two scalars from ASCII, U+00E9 and U+1F600, exhaustively over the exact 17,031-case domain. CI runs every harness above on each pull request (formal-kani, formal-kani-extended) except the string family, of which pull requests run a 20-case smoke subset and the weekly schedule runs all 17,031 cases (formal-kani-strings-ascii, -mixed, -pure); the string claim rests on the latest green weekly run. Every Kani-detected mutant (m2-m4, m9-m13, m22-m25) must be refuted by its named harness on each pull request (formal-mutants-fast); all 48 mutants run nightly (formal-mutants-full). Not claimed: parse_never_panics (not verified; parser panic-freedom is the parser-totality claim).
assumptions: harness bounds and feature selections in run-kani.sh (no default features; built with -Zinline-mir=no, so rustc's MIR inliner cannot bypass a stub)

std semantics, with two proof-only selections: A1 align_offset returning usize::MAX (documented as permitted) and G1 Vec::push restricted to its non-growth branch (fails closed; the negative control push_guard_is_in_force must fail on it before the default set runs)
numeric route guard stub in the integer harnesses (fail-closed, checked unreachable for numeric input)
Kani 0.68.0 / CBMC 6.11 and the bundled kissat 4.0.1
real unicode-normalization NFC inside the harnesses that parse strings

strong fairness of operator void

retention at least the capability lifetime in the safe configuration

no permanent database failure

the recorded responses are what those authorities send today; no scheduled job re-stamps at them
RSA signature verification by the rsa crate (public-key operations only)

SHA-256 collision resistance
Ed25519 signatures

claims.claim: The strongest completeness label remains conditional on truthful resource labeling. Project frontier and checkpoint writes now serialize through a persisted Postgres guard, tested with two pools and separate processes; full multi-instance deployment remains gated on a content store shared by replicas and a per-replica ingest budget; authenticated capability-project binding, scoped nonce claims and bounded recovery are built and run together in the two-process failure matrix (multi-writer-failure-matrix). claims.claim: Real averin-server processes on one PostgreSQL schema survive a scripted matrix of single failures with no invariant violation found by a trace monitor: one nonce used by racing requests over two processes, one use identity sent repeatedly, a prospective and a total revoke against a use that already read the revocation state, a use against an uncommitted revoke, kill -9 during an open prepare or finalize transaction, stranded broker_seq recovery while the other process writes and a recovery process killed between its fence and its terminal transaction, a lost COMMIT acknowledgment cut before and after the server committed (finalize, use and revoke, retried on both processes), and concurrent checkpoints. The monitor checks no use after an acknowledged revoke, one admission per nonce, no session fork, a numbered checkpoint chain ending at the committed frontier, no receipt at or after its cutoff, a gapless broker_seq log, and every acknowledged operation durable, and has negative controls. Sampled interleavings of two or three processes on one Postgres 16 schema, not a proof, and not a cluster: it excludes a content store shared by replicas, the per-replica ingest budget, an object-storage witness and Postgres failover, so the single-writer-per-project deployment policy stays.
assumptions: PostgreSQL serializes the project guard row
the TCP proxy sees the simple-query COMMIT of a project write transaction
all project writers use WithProjectWrite
the processes share one local content directory

claims.claim: Under the caller-selected db_serialized_v1 policy, historical_authorized_as_of_snapshot is satisfied only when every validated receipt carries a body-bound resource-signed authorization ordinal below its grant's authenticated prospective cutoff and at or below the watermark of an authenticated, fresh v2 revocation snapshot for the project. Current revocation still blocks ok, revoked_uses_blocked, authorized and the capstone under every policy; strict, total, legacy v1, stripped, stale or malformed evidence never yields a historical positive. The model theorem covers the claim kernel and support erasure, not the verifier's extraction passes; the order is Averin's database order, not physical action time.
assumptions: honest resource signer signs one ordinal per receipt in its committing transaction
honest revocation signer signs the boundary time and watermark it read
PostgreSQL serializes the project guard row
caller supplies a trustworthy evaluation time and freshness bound

claims.claim: record::seal returns Ok only for a body whose sealed form passes verify_sealed's top-level shape check, domain pin and canon_version pin (SB-29), and checkpoint::seal_checkpoint returns Ok only for a body whose sealed form passes verify_checkpoint_sealed's domain pin and canon_version pin, checked by deterministic property tests and, for the Go server producers that the server test suite reaches (records and checkpoints), by running the real cgo seal in enforce mode across that suite. Not a proof; does not cover nested object shape, unknown checkpoint keys, the checkpoint chain checks of validate_chain, hash or signature validity, or AVERIN_SEAL_SHAPE=shadow, which seals unverifiable records and checkpoints on purpose as a rollback switch.
assumptions: the finite deterministic generator builds the defect classes that matter
the Go suite reaches every producer kind it lists

claims.claim: The averin-verify bundle headline word and exit code equal the report's claim verdict (PASS needs a satisfied requested claim and externally pinned keys; CONSISTENT is the same claim under the bundle's own keys; INSUFFICIENT and FAIL otherwise), the same rule as verifier/claim-verdict.js; averin-verify record uses the same words and exit codes (PASS only under a key passed on the command line, CONSISTENT for a keyless record that checks out, FAIL when a check fails). A finite differential over the verdict oracle corpus plus end-to-end tests of the binary; not a proof, and it says nothing about whether the claims themselves are right.

claims.claim: averin's v3 subject digest and v3 signing preimage reproduce the cross-plane golden vectors in vectors/authority-v3.v1.json, which is repackaged from the executable Lean oracle and the golden vectors by scripts/vectors/gen_authority_v3.py. govder, which signs authority proofs, keeps a byte-identical copy pinned in vectors.lock. Examples only, not a proof; says nothing about approver identity.
assumptions: the oracle's expected bytes are generated from the Lean definitions the proofs are about

claims.claim: averin's hiding commitment (commit::commit) reproduces the 11 golden commitments in vectors/params-commitment.v1.json, which are generated by the independent Python reference scripts/vectors/gen_params_commitment.py. vultrino keeps a byte-identical copy pinned in vectors.lock. Examples only, not a proof; says nothing about nonce randomness or hiding.

claims.claim: For a v3 govder authority proof, averin re-derives the signed evidence_hash from the record's own fields including decided_by and a digest of the ordered sign-off set (extensions.govder.body.sign_offs), and reports the record when the signed evidence differs: evidence naming a different decider and a sign-off set reordered after signing are each refused. A record sealed before approver binding (its body names an approver, its signed evidence is the historical field set) stays valid history under the default verifier options: it raises no issue and its notes say that decided_by and the sign-off set are not committed by the evidence (the approver-binding-policy-fails-unbound claim covers the option that makes it an issue). The spelling is pinned by vectors/approver-evidence.v1.json, generated by an independent Python reference (scripts/vectors/gen_approver_evidence.py) and copied byte for byte into govder, whose signer reproduces every case. Historical v2 evidence keeps its original field set. Not that the named subjects are authenticated, are humans, are in a configured group or are distinct (an operator and broker property, XV-10); not that the approval is recent; not that a signer committed to the right names (a signer that signs evidence naming mallory over a record naming mallory is consistent, and a signer that omits the approver members is accepted as pre-binding history unless the caller requires binding, so the binding holds only for records whose signer includes them or where the policy is on); not NFC or escaping agreement beyond the vector cases. The subject digest already covers the whole record body; this adds the evidence commitment an offline verifier checks by re-derivation.
assumptions: the evidence spelling in vectors/approver-evidence.v1.json is the one govder's signer and averin's verifier both mean

claims.claim: GET /v2/posture sits under the ordinary project API-key auth (401 without the project's bearer on a keyed deployment) and reports from the running process whether the app API is keyed (an explicit open store counts as not keyed), whether the Postgres store is wired, whether the signing seed is the committed dev seed, whether AVERIN_REQUIRE_PROD_SECRETS is on, the two authority-pin switches, and the Go toolchain, git commit and (when the build script stamped it) rustc of the linked decision core. A real averin-server process, built and started in the test, reports the keyed in-memory deployment and reports the dev seed as such. It also reports the region label (AVERIN_REGION), the Postgres schema version the binary understands and whether startup verified the runtime database role. Booleans, a short region label, the schema version (an integer) and build identifiers only. Not that the database is reachable, that the keys are strong, that AVERIN_REQUIRE_PROD_SECRETS reaches a running binary (the live-process test cannot boot with it on without Postgres), or that a deployment calls the endpoint (the feir-os posture verifier does).
assumptions: the deployment's build script stamps the rustc version with -ldflags; an unstamped build reports none
the deploy-time verifier calls the endpoint with a project key

claims.claim: averin's recording key can be rotated without breaking history checks. The server stamps an operator-set epoch, publishes the current and every retired key with its status, and publishes signed rotation statements (new domain averin.key_rotation.v1) that link each retired key to its successor, refusing to start when the lineage is inconsistent. The verifier counts a statement as verified only when its signatures hold over keys the bundle lists, and extends an externally pinned key's trust to the successor only through a verified scheduled statement from a key that is neither revoked nor compromised; a compromise statement extends none. A bundle exported across a rotation by a real server verifies from the old key's pin alone and stops verifying when the statement is stripped. Not that the old key signed nothing after the rotation time (the operator destroys the old seed, or for a compromise a timestamp anchor taken before the compromise time decides), that the rotation happened at the stated time, or that the operator followed the runbook.
assumptions: the operator holds the old seed at a scheduled rotation and destroys it afterwards
the auditor pins the old key out of band and marks it compromised when it is
Ed25519 unforgeability

claims.claim: Prompt and answer text from the SDKs, the recording proxy and the MCP server is committed, not signed. The server moves input, output and rationale out of extensions.content_preview to the top level at ingest, so the signed body carries only salted hiding commitments, the text sits in the content store where a retention purge removes it, and the history still verifies after the purge. A content_preview that is not an object, carries another key, repeats a top-level field or sits on a body-bound v3 authority record is refused. The verifier reports how many records still carry cleartext content_preview (cleartext_content_records). Not that records sealed before this change are erased: their text is part of signed, chained bodies and stays; that personal data placed elsewhere in the body is committed; or that the Python SDK test runs in CI.
assumptions: the deployment sets AVERIN_CONTENT_DIR with a master key and AVERIN_RAW_RETENTION_DAYS, else nothing is purged
clients put the text in the three named fields or the legacy preview key

Not that a sending plane's key equals one of them (the comparison is feir-os evaluate.jq, tested against stub reports, and there is no keyed-averin four-plane run), that keys are strong or rotated, or that a fingerprint is private against a weak key.
assumptions: the deployment's build script stamps the rustc version with -ldflags; an unstamped build reports none
the deploy-time verifier calls the endpoint with a project key

Public keys only. Not that govder derives the same keys (feir-os evaluate.jq compares, tested against stub reports), or that any key is strong or rotated.
assumptions: the deployment's build script stamps the rustc version with -ldflags; an unstamped build reports none
the deploy-time verifier calls the endpoint with a project key

claims.claim: `averin-migrate --hook` is the idempotent pre-upgrade Job mode: it initializes an empty Postgres database, leaves one at the current schema version unchanged, refuses one newer than the binary, never bootstraps over an unstamped legacy schema, advances an older database only with both cutover roles (otherwise prints cutover_required and exits 3 without changing anything), and serializes concurrent runs on the advisory lock; `--check-runtime` runs the server's runtime-role check. claims.claim: A server with no auth store refuses every /v2 request with 401, and with scoped tokens a token is accepted only for its own project, before its not_after instant, and for the routes its role allows (read for GET and HEAD, write for the nine evidence-adding POST routes, admin for everything else, so an unclassified route fails closed). The server passes the project's pinned authority keys (project pin first, then the global pin, per source) to the verifier as authority_keys, so the record is read as verified or legacy-unbound instead of unverifiable. Not that export refuses (it reuses the verdict only for its completeness wording), and not that a project with no pinned authority key is covered: there the record is unverifiable and the policy has nothing to check.

claims.claim: Trusted timestamps are off unless an operator sets AVERIN_TSA_PRESET or AVERIN_TSA_URL; the freetsa preset is one setting and logs the signing key to pin; AVERIN_TSA_URL takes any other authority and AVERIN_TSA_AUTH_HEADER the credential header a paid one needs, which is refused at start-up unless the TSA URL is https; setting a preset and a URL together, or an unknown preset, is fatal at start-up. The client's request is byte-identical to the one FreeTSA, DigiCert and Sectigo accepted and unwraps each of their recorded responses to the recorded token. Not that an authority is reachable or that anchoring succeeds (a TSA outage stores the checkpoint un-anchored), and the pinned preset key is a trust decision the operator confirms.
assumptions: the operator pins the TSA key out of band before relying on an anchor
outbound HTTPS to the chosen authority is permitted

claims.claim: A month segment (bundle.segment, averin.segment.v1) verifies on its own: its base checkpoint is carried and checked like every checkpoint, the chain starts at that base, every checkpoint falls in the stated UTC month and the base before it, the latest frontier equals the segment's heads, its record_count equals the base's count plus the records carried and no carried record is a member of the base frontier, and a base the caller pinned must be the base stated. averin-verify chain additionally requires each month to start from the previous month's head, months and projects to agree, every parent a month points before its base to exist in an earlier month, and every grant or intent a use or outcome names across a month boundary to be held by an earlier month, and no record (by content hash or record id) to be carried by two months; it then verifies the months, put back together, as one whole-history bundle and its claim word is that whole history's, so a use with no matching grant or a second use of a single-use grant that spans months reaches the word as it does in one export (when that history fits the verifier's byte cap; over it the word is capped at INSUFFICIENT). A month reports the grant-log chain, federation heads and (with a base) cross_month_uses as not evaluated and never counts a cross-month use or outcome as matched; the chain's rebuilt history carries the latest month's revocation list and deployment attestation and every month's disclosures. Not that a month with parents before its base has a complete record set on its own (such a month reports record_completeness as not evaluated, and only the chain closes it), that earlier months are intact (only the chain over all of them says so), the use-to-grant predicate or the grant-log transparency chain inside one month, a revocation list or deployment attestation for a chain unless the latest month carries them (a server re-issues them for every month, split copies them into the last month only), the cross-month rules for a history over the byte cap (the word is then INSUFFICIENT, never PASS, and a cross-month double use in it is not reported as FAIL), a month with a base ruling out cross-month uses on its own (it lists cross_month_uses as not evaluated and is capped at INSUFFICIENT), or that a recorder showing different histories to different auditors is caught (that needs external anchoring).
assumptions: checkpoint created_ts is the recorder's own signed clock
Ed25519 unforgeability
records are cut by checkpoint record_count in insertion order

claims.claim: The server cuts a checkpoint from the latest checkpoint plus the records after it, and the body equals the one the full computation over the whole project would produce: sequence number and previous hash, record count (the base count plus the records after it), frontier (the base frontier minus the parents of the new records, plus the new records no new record names) and the grant-transparency head and per-broker head (the prior cumulative root folded over the grants after it, chained to the prior head). It refuses to sign when the new grants do not carry exactly the next broker_seq values, when the allocated maximum differs, when the store's record count differs from the base count plus the records after it, or when any page of the records after the base does not hold exactly the next ordinals in order (a record missing from the middle of the range), and it takes the full computation when there is no usable base. The cut whose checkpoint sequence number is a multiple of 100 (per project) and whose project has not had a shadow attempt in the last hour (so the scheduled shadow runs at most once per hour per project), the first incremental cut of a project after a process start, and every cut after a mismatch until restart, also compute the full body with the same timestamp and refuse to sign unless the two are identical; a refused sequence number is retried and shadow-checked again, so a restart does not let it through. A shadow that cannot run (the full computation errors, hits the statement timeout or exceeds its own time budget, 1 s by default and at most 20 s) does not refuse: the incremental body is signed, averin_checkpoint_shadow_failed_total is counted, an alert is logged and that project's next shadow waits for a backoff. The grant log counts a record as a grant only by exact-case keys and string values, as the verifier does. Not that the shadow keeps running as history grows (the full computation is O(history) and stops fitting its budget; the failed counter shows it, and from then on only the differential tests and the per-cut count and contiguity guards hold the equality), not that every unshadowed cut equals the full computation (the equality is argued in a code comment and checked on random histories; a divergence on an unshadowed cut is signed, because checkpoints are append-only, and is caught by the next shadowed cut of that project or by the verifier), that the latest stored checkpoint is intact (it is trusted as the base), that the full computation is cheap (it is O(history), used for the first cut and as the definition), or that a very large frontier costs nothing (every checkpoint carries it).
assumptions: records are insert-only and numbered in insertion order under the project write transaction
a record never names a later record as a parent
broker_seq allocation is MAX+1, idempotent per grant id, and a void fills only an unrecorded seq

claims.claim: GET /v2/records with after and order=asc serves the records after an insertion ordinal oldest first (at most 1000 per page) together, from one repeatable-read snapshot, with the store total, the latest checkpoint (seq, hash, record_count) and, on request, the checkpoint at a given seq (absent when there is none). A store error, an unreadable checkpoint count or a record ordinal gap (a page that is not exactly the ordinals after+1 onward) is a 500, a malformed request a 400, and the rows read are the page plus two checkpoint rows at any history size. Not that the records are authentic (nothing is verified and no bundle is built: a reader holds a read frontier bound to a signed checkpoint, not a verified one), that a rewrite below a reader's frontier is detected by this endpoint (the reader's own rolling re-read does that), that separate pages share a snapshot (a reader checks the continuity fields on every page), or that the Postgres plan uses the ordinal index in every case (the Postgres test counts rows and runs in the Postgres CI job).
assumptions: records are numbered in insertion order under the project write transaction
a checkpoint's record_count is the number of records it covers

claims.claim: The generic ingest path rejects every gateway refusal marker (event_type gateway_refusal, record_kind gateway-refusal, observed_via gateway, extensions.gateway_refusal, record_id prefix refusal-, idempotency_key prefix refusal:) with a 400, and an ordinary record still ingests. Not that POST /v2/refusals authenticates its caller beyond the write role (any project writer can submit a refusal), nor that a refusal reflects a real refusal: averin seals what the gateway reports.
assumptions: the server signing key signs a forged refusal exactly like a real one, so the reservation at ingest is the only defence

claims.claim: POST /v2/refusals builds the record from a closed body: an unknown field, an unknown class or entry point, a zero attempts count, a future last_at, an unsafe agent id and an inconsistent summary are a 400 that seals nothing; an unsafe action name is stored as invalid_name; a replay returns the same record; GET /v2/records filters by record_kind and exclude_record_kind. Not rate limiting of submissions, nor Postgres parity of the filtered page.
assumptions: the in-memory store backs these tests

claims.claim: The verifier counts gateway refusals (gateway_refusals, gateway_refusal_attempts, gateway_refusals_by_class) only for integrity-proven records with a valid shape, and counts a verbatim replayed record once. Not that the gateway reported every refusal: the count is a floor, Level 1 and Level 2 only, never Level 3.
assumptions: records are integrity-proven under the keys the caller pinned, or the bundle's own keys when none are pinned

claims.claim: A record with record_kind gateway-refusal whose shape is invalid (unknown class, entry point or key, zero attempts, divergent event_type, an authority block, broker evidence, an inconsistent summary, no extension) is a hard verification issue and is never counted. Not that a well-formed refusal is true.
assumptions: the closed vocabulary equals vectors/refusal-classes.v1.json

claims.claim: A real-producer capstone history with gateway refusals of ungranted actions stays attested complete over the brokered surface with the side-effect closure closed; the refusals are counted and add no resource, action pair or manifest entry. The committed fixture is signed by test-only keys (spec/test-keys.json). Not that any production taxonomy or manifest is signed: that is the separate FEI-36 release step.
assumptions: test-only keys derived from public labels sign the fixture

claims.claim: A generic record with event_type gateway_refusal and no record_kind is neither counted nor shape-checked; its bundle verifies with the same issues and proven count as the same bundle with an ordinary event_type. The verifier keys on record_kind. Not a quantification over every existing history.
assumptions: an older averin could seal a generic record with that event_type

claims.claim: The native verifier, the cgo FFI and the WASM verifier produce the same refusal fields for the four committed rows (refusals, legacy event_type only, unknown class, capstone with refusals). Not agreement on inputs outside those rows.
assumptions: the vectors are signed by test-only keys

proofs.symbol: WASM replays the gateway refusal vectors

claims.claim: On Postgres a seal reads the session's heads from the session_heads table, which PutRecord keeps in the record insert's own transaction (the new record's parents removed, the record added, only when a new row was inserted), instead of scanning the session; the table equals the full-scan definition after every insert of seeded random histories (forks, merges, forced and cross-session parents, duplicates, replays, collapses, many sessions) and after the migration backfill, and the read is one index lookup however long the session is. Not that it equals the full scan on every history (a record naming a parent not yet stored, whose parent arrives later, differs; the seal path does not produce it), not the in-memory store (it scans the session), not ProjectHeads, and not that a writer bypassing PutRecord keeps the table current.
assumptions: a project's writers are serialized by the project write guard
records are written only through Store.PutRecord

claims.claim: On Postgres and in the in-memory store, a use-outcome finds the intent it completes (Store.IntentRecord) and any outcome already completing it (Store.UseOutcomeFor) with lookups that equal the whole-session scan they replaced on seeded random histories (several sessions and projects, outcomes repeated for one intent, spoofed and kind-less generic records, wrongly typed fields, replays); on Postgres they are answered through records_project_record_id_uniq and the new records_use_outcome_intent_idx (migration 0010, schema version 10) instead of reading the session, so the cost of a metered call does not grow with the session's history, and a read error propagates. Not that they equal the scan on every history (JSON key names are matched exactly, where the scan's decoder is case-insensitive, so the lookup is at most stricter), not the in-memory store's cost (it scans), and not the planner's choice beyond the asserted plans.
assumptions: record_id is unique per project (PutRecord and records_project_record_id_uniq)
records are written only through Store.PutRecord, which assigns the insertion ordinal

claims.claim: averin-server refuses to start when AVERIN_DATABASE_URL is set (durable records), AVERIN_CONTENT_DIR is unset and AVERIN_DEV_MODE is off, with a message naming AVERIN_CONTENT_DIR and why, because the raw values behind selective disclosure would be held in memory only and lost on every restart while their records stay. With a content dir, with dev mode, or with no database the guard does not refuse. In dev mode the in-memory content store is bounded: past its byte cap (64 MiB by default, AVERIN_CONTENT_MEM_MAX_BYTES) it evicts the oldest blobs first, never holds more than the cap, and logs a warning when it evicts. Not that disclosures of evicted content still work (they do not), not the durable stores' own bounds, and not that the guard is the only way to lose content.
assumptions: the server is started through cmd/averin-server

claims.claim: A whole-history export or verify whose stored record and checkpoint JSON, with the bundle's fixed overhead, already exceeds the single-bundle limit is refused with the same 413 and body as before, from SQL aggregates (Postgres octet_length sums), before any record or checkpoint is loaded. The estimate is a lower bound of the serialized bundle on random histories, so a bundle the exact check would serve is never refused; an estimate within the limit falls through to the exact load-and-check, so the boundary is unchanged. Not month segments (they are checked on their own records), and not that the estimate is tight.
assumptions: records are written only through Store.PutRecord and checkpoints through Store.PutCheckpoint
